**Lac qui Parle County** ( _LAK kee PARL_)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-2) is a county in the southwestern part of the U.S. state of Minnesota. As of the 2020 census, the population was 6,719.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-QF-3) Its county seat is Madison.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-4) The largest city in the county is Dawson.
The name of the county is a French translation of the Dakota name, "Mde Iyedan," meaning "lake that speaks."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-7)
In 1862 the Minnesota legislature authorized creation of a county to be called Lac qui Parle on an area north of the Minnesota River. However, that initiative was not approved by the local voters affected, so the proposed county did not come into existence. Nine years later (March 6, 1871) the legislature authorized creation of the present Lac qui Parle County, south of the Minnesota River, and it was approved by local voters. The county seat was established at Lac qui Parle village.
In 1884 a settlement was platted at the railway stop in Madison Township (named for Madison, Wisconsin). The settlement, also named Madison, was incorporated in 1885, and in 1889 the county government was moved from Lac qui Parle village to this new town, which incorporated as a city in 1902.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-8)

In 1886, a county-wide election chose Madison as the county seat. 150 men and 40 teams of horses rode to Lac qui Parle village, where the town hall was at the time, and dragged the building to Madison.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-9)
A new county courthouse was built in Madison in 1899, and in 1903 the Madison City Hall was completed. A total of four fires swept the city's main area during the early years of the twentieth century, resulting in most wood structures in the area being replaced with brick buildings.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-Mad-10)
Until May 1965, when county option was eliminated, Lac qui Parle was a dry county; no beverages with over 3.2% alcohol could be sold.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-11)
A March 2011 study by the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation ranked this as Minnesota's healthiest county.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-13)
The county reached its peak population of 15,554 in 1920. However, the county seat continued its population growth until 1960, when 2,380 residents were counted.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-Mad-10)

Lac qui Parle County is on the west side of Minnesota. Its west border abuts the east border of the state of South Dakota. The Minnesota River flows southeastward along the county's NE border, creating Marsh Lake and Lac qui Parle Reservoir[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-14) The Minnesota River flow is augmented by Yellow Bank River near the county's north corner, and by Lac qui Parle River near the county's east border. The south fork of the Yellow Bank flows northward through the west portion of the county, and meets the north fork of the Yellow Bank in the north end of the county; the combined flow discharges into the Minnesota at the county's NE border. The Lac qui Parle flows eastward through the lower portion of the county, discharging into the Minnesota near the community of Lac qui Parle.
The county terrain consists of rolling hills, knolls and short bluffs near the west end, running to a steep bluff overlooking the Minnesota River valley on its east border. The area is largely devoted to agriculture.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-LQPCM-15) The terrain slopes to the north and east, with its highest point near its SW corner, at 1,404 ft (428 m) ASL.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-16) The county has a total area of 778 square miles (2,020 km 2), of which 765 square miles (1,980 km 2) is land and 13 square miles (34 km 2) (1.7%) is water.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-17)
The county's northern boundary is defined by the Minnesota River. Two tributaries, the Lac qui Parle River and the Yellow Bank River, flow through the county to discharge into the Minnesota.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-18)

Salt Lake is found the county's western border. The lake is the only alkaline lake in Minnesota.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-19) Salt Lake is a popular bird watching location[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-20) because it is home to 145 species of birds that are not found other places in the area. Rare plants and insects have also been known to inhabit the region.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-21)

About 32.9% of all households were made up of individuals and 16.9% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-Census2020DP-37)
There were 3,471 housing units, of which 14.9% were vacant. Among occupied housing units, 80.9% were owner-occupied and 19.1% were renter-occupied. The homeowner vacancy rate was 1.7% and the rental vacancy rate was 12.7%.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lac_qui_Parle_County,_Minnesota#cite_note-Census2020DP-37)

The racial makeup of the county was 98.85% White, 0.16% Black or African American, 0.22% Native American, 0.32% Asian, 0.06% from other races, and 0.38% from two or more races. 0.26% of the population were Hispanic or Latino of any race. 44.6% were of Norwegian and 35.2% German ancestry.

The average household size was 2.37 and the average family size was 2.96.
The county population contained 24.50% under the age of 18, 5.70% from 18 to 24, 22.70% from 25 to 44, 23.90% from 45 to 64, and 23.20% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 43 years. For every 100 females there were 98.60 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 95.60 males.
The median income for a household in the county was $32,626, and the median income for a family was $41,556. Males had a median income of $27,939 versus $19,681 for females. The per capita income for the county was $17,399. About 5.60% of families and 8.50% of the population were below the poverty line, including 7.80% of those under age 18 and 9.20% of those age 65 or over.
